title: G 550
verdict: The last G-Class sold new in America with a solid front axle. Underneath the chrome running boards it’s the same triple-locked tractor as ever — just with a bigger V8, a seven-speed and, from 2016, a pair of turbochargers.

paragraphs: The G 550 is the old G-Class at the height of its contradictions. By 2009 the boxy W463 cost north of a hundred grand, wore a navigation screen and was more likely to be photographed outside a gym than in a riverbed. Yet nothing that mattered had been diluted: a separate ladder frame, solid axles at both ends, permanent four-wheel drive with low range and three fully locking differentials. For the US the name changed and the engine grew; the truck itself carried on until 2018, when an all-new G with independent front suspension finally replaced it.

story.heading: A NEW NAME, A BIGGER V8
paragraphs: For 2009 the US-market [[g-class/g500|G 500]] became the G 550, swapping the 5.0-litre M113 for the 5.5-litre M273 V8: 382 hp and 391 lb-ft. The 722.9 seven-speed automatic had already replaced the old five-speed on the 2007 US G 500, so the G 550 arrived with seven ratios from the start. The 2008 update had also brought a new grille with three thicker horizontal fins and a COMAND APS system with its own off-road menu.

A later update lifted the dashboard and centre console from the ML-Class and added LED daytime running lamps, new mirrors, DISTRONIC cruise and blind-spot monitoring. Along the way came special editions — the 2011 Edition Select, a Japan-only G 550 Night Edition of 100 trucks, and a 30th-anniversary G 500/G 550 with designo leather — none of which changed the hardware underneath.

story.heading: TWIN TURBOS AND A LONG GOODBYE
paragraphs: For 2016 the naturally aspirated V8 gave way to the 4.0-litre twin-turbo M176, with its turbochargers tucked between the cylinder banks: 416 hp and 450 lb-ft. Mercedes-Benz USA quoted 0–60 mph in 5.8 seconds and an electronically limited 130 mph — for a 5,724-lb brick with the drag coefficient of a filing cabinet. The 2016 G 550 started at $119,900.

The off-road numbers barely moved over the decade: 9.3 inches of ground clearance, 23.6 inches of wading depth, 30° approach and departure angles and a 24° breakover, per Mercedes-Benz USA. The same twin-turbo engine went into the outrageous portal-axle [[g-class/4x4-squared|G 550 4×4²]] for 2017. Then, at Detroit in January 2018, Mercedes revealed the [[g-class/second-gen|second-generation G]] — and the solid front axle was gone.

story.heading: WHY OFF-ROADERS STILL WANT ONE
paragraphs: A solid front axle is a simple, strong, articulating thing, and it makes the G 550 the most modern G you can lift and tire the old-fashioned way. One Expedition Portal member put BFGoodrich KO2s in 275/70R18 on his stock-height 2014 G 550, with no rubbing even when flexing the axles in opposite directions, then added a Gobi roof rack — which knocked his fuel economy from about 12–13 mpg to 10–11.

The same owner later dropped the truck into a sinkhole in a creek. Recovery took about five hours, three tow services and, finally, a family member’s tractor; he noted the doors hadn’t leaked a drop. That’s the G 550 in a sentence: tougher than its reputation, and nowhere near as clever as a lifted [[land-cruiser/80-series|80 Series]] at avoiding trouble in the first place. Its contemporaries — the [[land-cruiser/200-series|Land Cruiser 200]], [[lexus/lx570|LX 570]] and [[range-rover/l322|Range Rover L322]] — were all softer, newer designs with independent fronts.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · ONE TRUCK, TWO HEARTS
callout.title: 5.5-litre or 4.0 twin-turbo?
paragraphs: 2009–2015 trucks use the M273 5.5-litre V8, a naturally aspirated engine shared with the S- and E-Class of the era. Its known weak points are well mapped: the map-controlled thermostat (the single most common failure, according to FCP Euro), intake-manifold swirl-flap levers, crankcase-breather seals and oil wicking up the camshaft-magnet connectors. The infamous idler-gear wear problem is attributed to early 2004–2008 production engines, which puts the G 550 largely after it — but scan for cam-timing codes anyway.

2016–2018 trucks get the M176 4.0-litre twin-turbo: 34 more horsepower and 59 more lb-ft, but turbos, intercooling and more heat in a tight engine bay. EPA fuel economy didn’t reward the change — every G 550 from 2010 to 2018 is rated 13 mpg combined — so choose on budget and service history, not on the window sticker.

engineering_intro: The G 550 is the end of the line for the original engineering recipe. The body bolts to a separate steel ladder frame; both axles are rigid, located by links and sprung on coils; steering is a hydraulically assisted recirculating-ball box. Power flows through a two-speed transfer case to all four wheels all the time, split 50:50, and three 100% differential locks — centre, rear, front — are engaged from switches on the dash.

engineering.note: Separate steel frame under the body, as on every G since 1979.
Link-located, coil-sprung. The last US G built this way.
Two-speed transfer case with a low range for crawling.
Three 100% locks — the G’s party trick since the W463 arrived in 1990.
Approach, departure, breakover (MY2016 Mercedes-Benz USA figures). 9.3 in clearance, 23.6 in wading.

engineering_note.title: BIGGER TIRES, RECODE THE TRUCK
engineering_note.body: Owners on Expedition Portal report that taller tires confuse the ESP and throw the speedometer off unless the tire size is re-coded with a Mercedes STAR/XENTRY diagnostic tool. One 2014 G 550 owner on 275/70R18s found the ESP stepping in noticeably earlier in quick corners and hard launches until it was addressed.

buying_checks.head: Decide on the engine first
buying_checks.body: 2009–2015 trucks have the naturally aspirated 5.5-litre M273; 2016–2018 trucks have the 4.0-litre twin-turbo M176. Same chassis, same lockers, different maintenance profile — and the 2016-on trucks command more money.

buying_checks.head: Test all three lockers
buying_checks.body: Engage centre, rear and front in order on a loose surface and watch the dash indicators. A truck whose lockers ‘were never used’ often has a vacuum or actuation fault waiting.

buying_checks.head: Watch the temperature gauge (M273)
buying_checks.body: A slow-to-warm or erratic coolant temperature, or codes P0597–P0599, points at the map-controlled thermostat — the most common M273 failure.

buying_checks.head: Scan for swirl-flap codes (M273)
buying_checks.body: P2004, P2005 or P2006 mean the intake-manifold flap mechanism has failed. Don’t ignore it: broken flap pieces can be ingested by the engine.

buying_checks.head: Look behind the front wheels
buying_checks.body: Gear oil on the inner wheels, calipers or rotors means leaking front axle seals — and possibly contaminated brakes.

buying_checks.head: Drive it at 55–70 mph
buying_checks.body: Wander, wheel shake or a vague on-centre feel usually means a worn steering damper and tired linkage — common on the solid-axle G.

buying_checks.head: Rust where nobody cleans
buying_checks.body: Tailgate lower edge, door bottoms, sills, rear frame tubes, strut mounts, inner wheel arches and around the rear bumper. Salt-belt trucks deserve a lift and a flashlight.

buying_checks.head: Check the headliner and the badges
buying_checks.body: A sagging headliner means water (usually blocked sunroof drains). And plenty of G 550s wear AMG bumpers and badges — check the VIN before paying a G 63 premium.

repairs.title: Thermostat (M273)
repairs.symptoms: Engine slow to warm up or running cool, erratic temperature gauge, poor heater output, codes P0597, P0598 or P0599. Note that 80–95 °C can be normal on a working map-controlled thermostat.
repairs.fix: Drain enough coolant to drop the level below the housing, unplug the thermostat’s electrical connector, release the hoses and unbolt the housing. If the history is unknown, replace the radiator hose at the same time — old hoses often seal poorly at the O-ring on the new part. Refill with Mercedes-approved coolant and bleed the system. FCP Euro suggests treating it as a roughly 60,000-mile wear item.
repairs.tools: Map-controlled thermostat · radiator hose · MB-approved coolant (genuine or Pentofrost NF) · Torx sockets · hose-clamp pliers · multimeter (heater element should read about 15.2 Ω ± 1.5 Ω)

repairs.title: Intake manifold swirl flaps (M273)
repairs.symptoms: Check-engine light with P2004, P2005 or P2006; sometimes a lumpy idle or flat spot. The operating lever on the flap shaft breaks.
repairs.fix: Repair kits for the lever exist, but FCP Euro recommends replacing the complete manifold assembly because the flaps can also fail internally and send pieces into the cylinders. Remove the engine cover and air intake, disconnect the throttle body and sensors, unbolt the manifold, fit the new one with new gaskets, and clear the codes.
repairs.tools: Intake manifold assembly (e.g. Pierburg) · manifold gaskets · Torx and hex sockets · torque wrench · scan tool

repairs.title: Crankcase breather & oil-cooler seals (M273)
repairs.symptoms: Oil residue around the breather cover’s screws; in bad cases a burning-oil smell in the cabin as oil drips onto the exhaust manifold. A grimy belt tensioner hints at oil-cooler seal seepage.
repairs.fix: Replace the plastic breather cover/O-ring assembly — the rubber O-ring is what hardens and leaks. If the oil cooler is weeping, replace its seals at the same time and degrease the area so you can confirm the fix.
repairs.tools: Breather cover assembly · oil-cooler seal kit · Torx/external-Torx bits (early vs later engines differ) · brake cleaner

repairs.title: Oil in the cam-magnet connectors
repairs.symptoms: Oil inside the camshaft-adjuster magnet connectors; on neglected engines oil wicks up the harness toward the engine control unit.
repairs.fix: Unplug each connector and inspect for oil. Replace leaking cam magnets and fit Mercedes’ sacrificial adapter pigtails so any future seepage stops short of the main harness. Clean contaminated connectors with electrical cleaner.
repairs.tools: Camshaft-adjuster magnets · factory sacrificial pigtails · electrical contact cleaner · Torx bits

parts.name: Camshaft adjuster magnet repair kit (OE supplier, G 550 2009–2015)

repairs.title: Diff locks won’t engage
repairs.symptoms: One or all locks refuse to engage or drop out, indicator lights flash or stay off. On trucks with vacuum-actuated locking, the fault is usually a leak, not the differential.
repairs.fix: Follow the same path MBWorld owners use on earlier W463s: confirm vacuum at the transfer case, then work back through the reservoir, lines and switchover valves with a gauge teed into each segment until you find the split line or connector. Exercise the locks regularly once fixed — disuse is their enemy.
repairs.tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · vacuum tees and line · replacement connectors

repairs.title: Front axle seal leak
repairs.symptoms: Gear oil on the inner front wheels, a gear-oil smell, oil on a caliper or rotor, brakes pulling to one side.
repairs.fix: Replace both front axle seals even if only one is leaking, and check the shafts for scoring. If oil reached the brakes, replace the pads and resurface or replace the rotors — contaminated pads are a safety issue.
repairs.tools: Genuine axle seals (both sides) · seal driver · gear oil · brake pads and rotors if contaminated

parts.name: Genuine Mercedes front axle shaft seal 009 997 28 47
Red Line 75W-90 GL-5 gear oil (listed for 2009–2014 G 550)

repairs.title: Steering damper & highway wander
repairs.symptoms: Highway wander, wheel shake at 55–70 mph, vague on-centre feel, clunks over bumps.
repairs.fix: Swap the steering damper for an OEM or upgraded unit (Bilstein B6 is a common choice), check the drag link and tie-rod ends for play, then get a front-end alignment.
repairs.tools: Steering damper · sockets and wrenches · tie-rod or drag-link ends if worn

parts.name: King steering stabilizer kit for W463

repairs.title: Cracked coil springs
repairs.symptoms: A loud thump over bumps, uneven ride height — often discovered after cold weather.
repairs.fix: Replace springs in axle pairs. If a lift is on the cards, do it now with a matched spring-and-shock kit rather than buying stock springs twice.
repairs.tools: Springs (pairs) · jack and stands · spring compressor if your setup needs one · new shocks recommended

parts.name: ARB Old Man Emu 50 mm lift springs for W463

faq.q: What’s the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: About 33 inches — a 275/70R18 on 18-inch wheels. A 2014 G 550 owner on Expedition Portal ran BFGoodrich KO2s in that size at stock height with no rubbing at full flex, and a G 500 owner rubbed only on aftermarket ET63-offset wheels (ET43 was fine). A 285/65R18 can rub slightly at full left lock; a 265/65R18 (about 31.6 in) fits with room to spare. Later trucks came on 19s–21s, and owners warn 18s don’t clear every caliper — check before buying wheels, and have the tire size re-coded.

faq.q: What size are the factory tires?
faq.a: A 2012 G 550 came on 265/60R18; optional sizes listed for that year run 275/55R19, 275/50R20 and 295/40R21. An Expedition Portal owner measured his 2017 G 550’s stock tires at about 30.5 inches tall.
7,000 lb with a braked trailer for a 2012 G 550. Check your own truck’s manual and hitch rating.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Bad. EPA figures for 2012 are 12 mpg city, 15 highway, 13 combined on premium — and every G 550 from 2010 to 2018 is rated 13 combined, twin-turbo or not. A roof rack cost one owner a couple more mpg.
faq.src: EPA VIA MPG BUDDY · EXPEDITION PORTAL

faq.q: How big is the fuel tank?
faq.a: 25.4 gallons, on both the 2012 G 550 and the 2017 4×4² spec sheets.

faq.q: Should I buy a 5.5-litre or a 4.0 twin-turbo?
faq.a: The 2016–2018 M176 twin-turbo has 416 hp and 450 lb-ft versus 382 hp and 391 lb-ft for the 2009–2015 M273, but EPA economy is identical. The M273’s faults are well documented and DIY-friendly; the twin-turbo is quicker and newer. Service history matters more than the engine choice.

faq.q: Does the M273 balance-shaft/idler-gear problem affect the G 550?
faq.a: It’s associated with early-production 2004–2008 M272 and M273 engines, which largely predates the 2009 G 550. If you see codes such as P0059, P0060, P0064 or P0272–P0276, or Mercedes codes 1200/1208, have it checked anyway.

faq.q: Can I use the diff locks on pavement?
faq.a: No. Locked differentials stop the wheels turning at different speeds, so on grippy surfaces the driveline binds and tires scrub. Lock on dirt, sand, snow or rock at low speed, and unlock before you’re back on tarmac.

faq.q: How much ground clearance and wading depth does it have?
faq.a: 9.3 inches of ground clearance and 23.6 inches of wading depth, with 30° approach and departure angles and a 24° breakover, per Mercedes-Benz USA for the 2016 G 550.

faq.q: Will it fit in my garage?
faq.a: A 2016 G 550 is 76.9 inches tall, 80.9 inches wide and about 187.6 inches long, on a 112.2-inch wheelbase. Add a roof rack and measure again.

The frame, axles and drivetrain are tough; the age-related jobs are predictable — thermostat and swirl flaps on the 5.5, axle seals, steering damper, locker actuation, rust and sunroof drains. A truck with receipts for those beats a low-mileage one that’s never been touched.

mods.why: A 2–3 inch lift with matched shocks clears 33s comfortably and stops a loaded truck sagging.
Flat platforms for a tent, recovery boards and fuel — with a wind deflector unless you like whistling.
Complete travel-ready builds — lift, armor, racks, lighting, storage — done as one coherent truck.
Kits that bring 4×4²-style stance and capability to a W463.
Specialists who know where W463s rust and how their lockers fail.
Swapping 19–21-inch rims for 18s with a taller all-terrain sidewall is the single most transformative change — check caliper clearance first.

baseline_service.intro: A G 550 that’s changed hands has usually been serviced for the showroom, not the trail — assume nothing below the engine has been touched and baseline every fluid. Split the list by engine first: 2009–2015 trucks have the 5.5-litre M273, 2016–2018 trucks the 4.0 twin-turbo M176, and many parts differ.

items.note: Both engines use a cartridge filter in a housing on top of the engine — replace the cap O-ring and drain-plug washer every time.
